Another storm, another flood: Some Ottawa residents report second basement flooding this summer

They're asking questions about whether City of Ottawa infrastructure can keep up with the wettest summer on record.

Author of the article:
By Natasha Baldin
Published Aug 12, 2026
Last updated 9 hours ago
5 minute read
Join the conversation

For Adrienne ten Cate, every rainy day now comes with the unwelcome ritual of running down to the basement to make sure more water hasn’t managed to find its way in.

Article content

After around 50 centimetres of water poured into her basement during the massive July 1 storm, damaging appliances and flipping plastic bins filled with family mementos upside down, the mere prospect of flooding happening again has kept her family on high alert.

Article content
Article content
Article content

“It’s really unnerving,” ten Cate told the Ottawa Citizen. “Psychologically, it’s difficult because now we’re going to worry every time it rains. You just can’t leave anymore — you don’t want to be gone because what if (flooding) happens while you’re away?”

Article content

Article content

For more than a month, it seemed like that basement monitoring was nothing more than an act of hypervigilance. Their home in Ottawa’s Qualicum neighbourhood stayed dry through multiple rainstorms, making the Canada Day flooding seem like an unlucky break from a 100-year storm.

Article content

That was until Aug. 10, when the family’s routine basement check revealed that the laundry room floor was again covered in a few centimetes of water.

Article content

Environment Canada recorded 23.5 millimetres of rain at the Ottawa Airport on Aug. 10 — around one-fifth of the July 1 rainfall total — as severe thunderstorms sparked tornado warnings in the area. That ensured that Ottawa had experienced its wettest summer since rainfall data was first collected in 1872, with 488 millimetres of precipitation received as of that date.

Article content
Article content

While still navigating insurance claims and remediation, more than $44,000 in out-of-pocket expenses and ongoing cleanup work from the first flood six weeks earlier, ten Cate family members feels like they’re having to start again.

Article content
Article content

“There were several other places where water was trickling in, and we’re not understanding what’s changed and why this is happening,” Adrienne ten Cate said. “All these price tags (from July 1), we now have to add to that what it’s going to cost to fix every one of those little hairline cracks that we’re seeing now.”

Article content

Article content

If there was one bright side, no belongings were damaged this time. The ten Cates’ basement was still gutted following the July 1 flood, and the precautionary move of installing a brand-new washer and dryer on 25-centimetre pedestals paid dividends.

Article content

The City of Ottawa said it received 111 service requests for basement flooding and 93 service requests related to flooded streets and catch basins between Aug. 10 at 3 p.m. and Aug. 11 at 3 p.m., with more than 87 per cent of basement flooding reports concentrated in the city’s west and southwest ends, specifically in College, Bay, Knoxdale-Merivale and River wards.

Article content

Those reports were “significantly lower” than they had been during the July 1 storm, noted Carol Hall, the city’s manager of water linear systems, with the Aug. 10 storm bringing 95 per cent fewer basement flood reports and 76 per cent fewer flooded street reports than the same 24-hour time frame starting July 1.

Article content

“During Monday’s rainfall, city crews monitored drainage infrastructure closely and proactively inspected catch basins and outlets to help manage stormwater runoff,” Hall wrote. “Temporary water pooling on streets is expected during periods of heavy rainfall and is often a sign that the stormwater system is working as designed.”

Article content

After coming home from his son’s karate lessons on Aug. 10, Bells Corners resident Thomas Coulson also returned to water in his basement for the second time this summer.

Article content

“Luckily, I didn’t have a ton of water, and there’s nothing in my basement because it’s still cleared out from when we did the first big cleaning of everything (after July 1),” Coulson said, adding he came home to a puddle about three centimetres deep and a metre wide.

Article content

As he again found himself in the basement cleaning up water with a Shop-Vac, Coulson started wondering whether basement flooding would become a childhood norm for his now six-and-a-half and 19-month-old kids.

Article content

“I’m trying to tuck my kid into bed, and I have to tell him he has to lay there by himself because I’m Shop-Vac-ing the basement again,” he said. “And now my kid is wondering, every time it rains, if we have to check the house. I don’t want him to have to worry about it every time it’s raining.”

Article content
Article content

Basement flooding has never been a recurring problem for both ten Cate and Coulson before this summer, leaving them with questions about the underlying damage the Canada Day storm may have caused to their homes and to city infrastructure.

Article content

“I understand that (July 1) was a big deal, and the flooding that happened was pretty widespread,” Coulson said. “But to have a 15-minute shower that’s a pretty typical little summer storm, I would say, and to have water come back in already, I don’t understand. That part is kind of perplexing to me.”

Article content

College ward Coun. Laine Johnson said she was on the phone with the city’s general manager of infrastructure services the morning after the Aug. 10 storm, asking questions about catch-basin capacity as the ground remained saturated.

Article content

“I know the City of Ottawa is extremely committed to getting this information to residents, and it’s a matter of getting it right,” Johnson said. “And, from what folks have experienced, there’s been overland flooding, sewer backup, ground-table saturation, all these different ways that people can flood, and often multiple ways that people did flood. So, to pick apart those variables is going to take some time.”

Article content
Article content

Johnson added she’d asked for “some meat and bones” on the timeline of the full infrastructure assessment, adding she’d like to see both short- and long-term upgrades considered as part of the 2027 city budget process.

Article content

While basement flooding numbers weren’t a major outlier following the Aug. 10 storm, Johnson said most of the reports to 311 and to her office were from residents concerned about flooding on the streets as sewers backed up and creeks overflowed.

Article content
Article content

For ten Cate, one of the most unnerving things has been seeing streets turn into rivers and local parks transform into lakes every time it rains as it seems city infrastructure struggles to keep up with Ottawa’s wettest summer on record.

Article content

“I understand that some of it is something structural that has happened to our house we can fix, but what about our roads?” she asked. “Did something get damaged somewhere that we’re not being told about or hasn’t been discovered yet?”

Article content
